name: Treaty with the Creeks, etc., 1856 (Creek and Seminole)
aka: Treaty with the Creek and Seminole, 1856
promises: The United States solemnly guaranteed the Seminole their new country and the Creek theirs, held by the same title as the 1832 and 1833 treaties and the 1852 patent (Article 3).

No State or Territory would ever pass laws for the government of the Creek or Seminole, and no part of either country would ever be included in or annexed to a Territory or State without the free consent of the tribe's legislature (Article 4).
$1,000,000 to the Creek Nation for the cession of land to the Seminole and the release of all Creek claims (Article 6).
The Creeks and Seminoles secured in the unrestricted right of self-government and full jurisdiction over persons and property within their limits, with intruders removed (Article 15).
Protection from hostile invasion and from aggression by other Indians and white persons, with full indemnity (Article 18).

breaches.what: The Curtis Act abolished the Creek tribal courts and transferred all pending civil and criminal cases to the federal courts of Indian Territory, overriding the self-government and jurisdiction secured by Article 15. The Supreme Court in McGirt names this among the ways Congress intruded on the Creeks' promised right to self-governance.

breaches.what: The Supreme Court, quoting this treaty's promise that no part of the Creek Reservation would be included in any Territory or State, held the reservation was never disestablished, while recognizing that Congress broke many of its promises to the Creek, including by abolishing the tribal courts in 1898.

breaches.what: The Indian Claims Commission held that the release in this treaty of the Creek claim for land taken by the 1814 Treaty of Fort Jackson was no bar to that claim, because the consideration given for the release was unconscionable; the Creek received in effect nothing for it.

compensation: Article 6 promised the Creek Nation $1,000,000 for the Seminole cession and the release of all claims. The Indian Claims Commission found in 1952 that the land ceded to the Seminole alone was worth more than that sum.
today: In McGirt v. Oklahoma (2020) the Supreme Court held the Creek Reservation, whose title this treaty confirmed, remains Indian country for purposes of federal criminal law. The Muscogee (Creek) Nation's Attorney General says its reservation boundaries have not been disestablished.

nationVoice.summary: The Nation's Office of the Attorney General states that McGirt confirmed its reservation boundaries were never disestablished and that the reservation remains Indian country under federal law.

openQuestions: The Curtis Act statute text itself was not opened; section 28 and the page citation come from McGirt (30 Stat. 504-505) and the Oklahoma Historical Society entry.

Whether the inclusion of Creek and Seminole lands in the State of Oklahoma in 1907 breached Article 4 without tribal legislative consent needs a reading of the 1901 Creek and 1897 Seminole agreements.

The Seminole Nation of Oklahoma own account of this treaty was not found. Evidence the other way: the Indian Claims Commission dismissed a Seminole claim for 1856-treaty annuities withheld in 1862-1866 (Docket 205, 7 November 1963, https://cdm17279.contentdm.oclc.org/digital/collection/p17279coll10/id/601) and rejected the argument that the 1861 withdrawal of federal troops forced the Seminole into the Confederacy (Docket 152, 22 August 1962, https://cdm17279.contentdm.oclc.org/digital/collection/p17279coll10/id/148).
Whether the Seminoles in Florida that Article 9 sought to remove were ever moved under it was not researched.

Audit 2026-11-08: the Curtis Act breach now cites McGirt (the primary reading) instead of the Oklahoma Historical Society entry, and drops "required presidential approval of later tribal legislation": McGirt attributes that requirement to the 1901 Creek Allotment Agreement (31 Stat. 872), not the Curtis Act, while the encyclopedia attributes it to the Curtis Act. The encyclopedia stays in sources.
